S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.

subtypes.Contamination Obsessions: Recurrent and intrusive worries about contamination, germs, or dirt.
subtypes.Pathological Doubt: Pathological doubt regarding safety or mistakes, such as whether doors are locked or gas valves are closed.
subtypes.Symmetry and Exactness Obsessions: A strong urge that items must be lined up exactly or be symmetrical.
subtypes.Forbidden or Taboo Thoughts: Intrusive thoughts involving aggressive (harming others), sexual, or religious content that are prohibited.
subtypes.Somatic Obsessions: Persistent and specific fear that one might have a serious disease.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.

subtypes.Cleaning or Washing Compulsions: Repetitive acts to remove contamination, such as hand washing, showering, or excessive cleaning.
subtypes.Checking Compulsions: Repeatedly checking items like door locks, gas stoves, or switches to prevent danger.
subtypes.Ordering and Arranging Compulsions: Organizing objects in a specific order or at a precise angle to reduce anxiety.
subtypes.Mental Acts: Mental rituals performed internally, such as praying, counting, or repeating specific words silently.
subtypes.Repeating Rituals: Repeating specific actions (e.g., standing up, passing through a door) a set number of times.

symptom.disease_info: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) is characterized by the presence of obsessions, compulsions, or both, which are time-consuming or cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning. Obsessions are recurrent, intrusive thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as unwanted and typically generate marked anxiety or disgust, while compulsions are repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed to reduce this distress or prevent a feared event, despite being excessive or not realistically connected. Onset is often in adolescence or early adulthood and tends to follow a chronic, waxing-and-waning course, frequently exacerbated by stress, responsibility increases, or role transitions. It is distinguished from related conditions such as generalized anxiety disorder (more free-floating worry), psychotic disorders (lack of insight, delusional conviction), and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (ego-syntonic perfectionism without intrusive thoughts) by the ego-dystonic, intrusive nature of obsessions and the ritualistic responses to them.

patient.personality: Kevin is a meticulous, reliability-focused technician who enjoys complex technical challenges, outdoor adventures, and creative hobbies like photography and music, and tends to push himself hard to get every detail right.
patient.stressor: Kevin traces the start of his difficulties to a period two years ago when his station underwent a major rebrand and he was promoted, informally, to be the de facto lead on several high-stakes live broadcasts. The new role meant longer hours, tighter timelines, and a sense that any technical mistake on his part would be visible to thousands of viewers and could jeopardize his reputation and team. As he took on designing system upgrades and supervising more junior staff, he found himself increasingly preoccupied with the possibility of catastrophic failures, replaying worst-case scenarios in his mind even during his off hours and on weekend hikes. Over time this constant mental checking and second-guessing began to slow his work, cut into his sleep as he stayed up re-reviewing setups and documentation, and caused friction at home when his spouse noticed he was mentally “still at the studio,” which finally led him to seek psychiatric help when he realized he could no longer trust himself to stop these thoughts on his own.
patient.chief_complaint: “I keep getting these intrusive thoughts about things going wrong at work, and I can’t switch them off no matter how much I tell myself everything’s fine.”

S065.name: Obsessions
S065.description: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are experienced as intrusive and unwanted, and attempts to ignore or suppress them.
S065.manifestation: It’s like there’s this nonstop loop in my head where I keep seeing the control room crashing during a live show because of some tiny thing I missed—an unplugged cable, a wrong patch, a mislabeled channel—and no matter how many times I remind myself we got through the broadcast fine, the thought pops back up and I start replaying every step in my mind, over and over, trying to prove to myself it’s not true.

S066.name: Compulsions
S066.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to an obsession or to prevent anxiety/distress; clearly excessive or not realistically connected.
S066.manifestation: To calm myself down, I end up re-checking the audio routing, light cues, and safety backups way more than is reasonable—sometimes I’ll stay an extra hour after a rehearsal just to run through the same checklist three or four times in the exact same order, or lie in bed mentally going through each switch and setting until I repeat it “right” enough times that I can finally fall asleep.
